q-95053.name: Question 1
q-95053.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy)\,j \\  & =(2x+y)\,i+x\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1$ and $y=-{t}^{2}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(2t+2-{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-{t}^{2})\,j \\  & =\,i-2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =((2t+2-{t}^{2})\,i+(t+1)\,j)\cdot (\,i-2t\,j) \\  & =2t+2-{t}^{2}-2t(t+1) \\  & =2t+2-{t}^{2}-2{t}^{2}-2t \\  & =2-3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

If f(x,y)=x2+xy and r(t)=(t+1)i−t2j, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2−3t2
b
 4t−t2
c
3+3t−t2
d
 2−4t
e
2+4t−3t2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂x(x2+xy)i+∂∂y(x2+xy)j=(2x+y)i+xj

Next, we substitute x=t+1 and y=−t2 into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=(2t+2−t2)i+(t+1)j

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t+1)i+ddt(−t2)j=i−2tj.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((2t+2−t2)i+(t+1)j)⋅(i−2tj)=2t+2−t2−2t(t+1)=2t+2−t2−2t2−2t=2−3t2.

q-167406.name: Question 2
q-167406.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}{e}^{x-y}\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}{e}^{x-y}\,j \\  & ={e}^{x-y}\,i-{e}^{x-y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2}$ and $y=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i-\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,i-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\,j)\cdot (2t\,i-\,j) \\  & ={e}^{{t}^{2}+t}\cdot 2t+(-{e}^{{t}^{2}+t})\cdot (-1) \\  & =(2t+1){e}^{{t}^{2}+t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If f(x,y)=ex−y and r(t)=t2i−tj, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
2tet2+t
b
(2t+1)et2+t
c
(t+1)et2−t
d
t2et2−t
e
(t−2)et2+t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y):

∇f(x,y)=∂∂xex−yi+∂∂yex−yj=ex−yi−ex−yj

Next, we substitute x=t2 and y=−t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=et2+ti−et2+tj

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t2)i+ddt(−t)j=2ti−j.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(et2+ti−et2+tj)⋅(2ti−j)=et2+t⋅2t+(−et2+t)⋅(−1)=(2t+1)et2+t.

q-95051.name: Question 3
q-95051.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{4}-{y}^{4})\,j \\  & =4{x}^{3}\,i-4{y}^{3}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(4{cos}^{3}⁡t\,i-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\,j)\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{3}⁡t-4{sin}^{3}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

q-95055.name: Question 4
q-95055.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}y)\,j \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}y}{{x}^{3}y}\,i+\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}y}\,j \\  & =\frac{3}{x}\,i+\frac{1}{y}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t$ and $y={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\frac{3}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j \\  & =\,i+{e}^{t}\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\frac{3}{t}\,i+\frac{1}{{e}^{t}}\,j)\cdot (\,i+{e}^{t}\,j) \\  & =\frac{3}{t}+\frac{{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{3}{t}+1 \\  & =\frac{t+3}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-95075.name: Question 6
q-95075.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z(x+y))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(z(x+y))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(z(x+y))\,k \\  & =z\,i+z\,j+(x+y)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & ={e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =({e}^{t}\,i+{e}^{t}\,j+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,k)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & ={e}^{t}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+{e}^{t}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t-{e}^{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =2{e}^{t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

∇f(r(t))=eti+etj+(sin⁡t+cos⁡t)k

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

q-167463.name: Question 7
q-167463.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))\,k \\  & =yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,i+xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,j+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y=2t$ and $z=\frac{1}{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t})\,k \\  & =\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,j+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,k)\cdot (\,i+2\,j-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}\,k) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 2+2{t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}}) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

If f(x,y,z)=sin⁡(xyz) and r(t)=ti+2tj+1tk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
4cos⁡(2t)−cos⁡t
b
4cos⁡(2t)
c
cos⁡(2t)+1t
d
2cos⁡(2t)
e
(2+2t)cos⁡(2t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(sin⁡(xyz))i+∂∂y(sin⁡(xyz))j+∂∂z(sin⁡(xyz))k=yzcos⁡(xyz)i+xzcos⁡(xyz)j+xycos⁡(xyz)k

Next, we substitute x=t, y=2t and z=1t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=2cos⁡(2t)i+cos⁡(2t)j+2t2cos⁡(2t)k

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(2t)j+ddt(1t)k=i+2j−1t2k.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2cos⁡(2t)i+cos⁡(2t)j+2t2cos⁡(2t)k)⋅(i+2j−1t2k)=2cos⁡(2t)⋅1+cos⁡(2t)⋅2+2t2cos⁡(2t)⋅(−1t2)=2cos⁡(2t)+2cos⁡(2t)−2cos⁡(2t)=2cos⁡(2t).

q-95143.name: Question 8
q-95143.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z)\,k \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,i-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,j+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡z}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡z}\,k \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡y\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,$ $y={t}^{2}$ and $z={e}^{t}$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,k \\  & =i+2t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{cot}⁡t\,i-\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}\,k)\cdot (i+2t\,j+{e}^{t}\,k) \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡t-2t\operatorname{tan}⁡{t}^{2}+{e}^{t}\operatorname{cot}⁡{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36238.name: Question 9
q-36238.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy+yz+xz)\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy+yz+xz)\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}(xy+yz+xz)\,k \\  & =(y+z)\,i+(x+z)\,j+(y+x)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t,y={e}^{t},$ and $z=e$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{t})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(e)\,k \\  & =i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(({e}^{t}+e)\,i+(t+e)\,j+({e}^{t}+t)\,k)\cdot (i+{e}^{t}\,j+(0)\,k) \\  & =({e}^{t}+e)\cdot 1+(t+e)\cdot {e}^{t}+({e}^{t}+t)\cdot 0 \\  & ={e}^{t}+e+t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t+1} \\  & ={e}^{t+1}+(1+t){e}^{t}+e.\end{aligned}
$$

a

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

Next, we substitute x=t,y=et, and z=e into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=(et+e)i+(t+e)j+(et+t)k

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is

r′(t)=ddt(t)i+ddt(et)j+ddt(e)k=i+etj+(0)k.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=((et+e)i+(t+e)j+(et+t)k)⋅(i+etj+(0)k)=(et+e)⋅1+(t+e)⋅et+(et+t)⋅0=et+e+tet+et+1=et+1+(1+t)et+e.

q-95074.name: Question 10
q-95074.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,j+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+2{z}^{2})\,k \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j+4z\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=t+1,$ $y=t-1$ and $z=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =2(t+1)\,i+2(t-1)\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-1)\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =i+j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2(t+1)\,i+2(t-1)\,j+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k)\cdot (i+j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k) \\  & =2(t+1)\cdot 1+2(t-1)\cdot 1+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =2t+2+2t-2+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4(t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t).\end{aligned}

Question 10

If f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+2z2 and r(t)=(t+1)i+(t−1)j+sin⁡tk, compute ddt[f(r(t))].

a
4(t+sin⁡tcos⁡t)
b
 2(2t2−sin⁡t)
c
 2sin⁡2t
d
2(t2−1)+cos⁡t
e
 t(1+sin⁡tcos⁡t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

First, we need to compute ∇f(x,y,z):

∇f(x,y,z)=∂∂x(x2+y2+2z2)i+∂∂y(x2+y2+2z2)j+∂∂z(x2+y2+2z2)k=2xi+2yj+4zk

Next, we substitute x=t+1, y=t−1 and z=sin⁡t into the above to find ∇f(r(t)):

∇f(r(t))=2(t+1)i+2(t−1)j+4sin⁡tk

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(t+1)i+ddt(t−1)j+ddt(sin⁡t)k=i+j+cos⁡tk.

Finally, applying the chain rule, we get

ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(2(t+1)i+2(t−1)j+4sin⁡tk)⋅(i+j+cos⁡tk)=2(t+1)⋅1+2(t−1)⋅1+4sin⁡t⋅cos⁡t=2t+2+2t−2+4sin⁡tcos⁡t=4(t+sin⁡tcos⁡t).

q-94874.name: Question 11
q-94874.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+\frac{x}{x+y})i+\frac{x}{x+y}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=1-2t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2t+1-2t)+\frac{2t}{2t+1-2t})i+\frac{2t}{2t+1-2t}\,j \\  & =2t\,i+2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-2t)\,j \\  & =2\,i+(-2)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2t\,i+2t\,j)\cdot (2\,i+(-2)\,j) \\  & =2t\cdot 2+2t\cdot (-2) \\  & =4t-4t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\sqrt{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\sqrt{2}))] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

q-94880.worked_solution:
The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡y\,i+\frac{x}{1+{y}^{2}}\,j.
$$

First, we substitute $x={t}^{2}+1$ and $y=t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+\frac{{t}^{2}+1}{1+{t}^{2}}\,j \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+j\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+1)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)\,j \\  & =2t\,i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\,i+j)\cdot (2t\,i+j) \\  & =\operatorname{arctan}⁡t\cdot 2t+1\cdot 1 \\  & =2t\operatorname{arctan}⁡t+1.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =2(1)\operatorname{arctan}⁡1+1 \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}+1 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}+1 \\  & =\frac{\pi +2}{2}.\end{aligned}

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$

In addition, we've been given that

$$
∇f(x,y)=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,i+\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,j.

First, we substitute $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ into $∇f(x,y)$ to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$

$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j)\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, evaluating the above at $t=\frac{\pi }{4},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

Evaluate ddt[f(r(t))] at t=π2 given that ∇f(x,y)=sin⁡yi+xcos⁡yj and r(t)=t2i+tj.

a
−1
b
0
c
2−π
d
12
e
π4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The chain rule in vector form states that ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t).

In addition, we've been given that ∇f(x,y)=sin⁡yi+xcos⁡yj.

First, we substitute x=t2 and y=t into ∇f(x,y) to find ∇f(r(t)): ∇f(r(t))=sin⁡ti+t2cos⁡tj.

Now, we calculate the derivative of r(t), which is r′(t)=ddt(t2)i+ddt(t)j=12i+j.

Applying the chain rule, we get ddt[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))⋅r′(t)=(sin⁡ti+t2cos⁡tj)⋅(12i+j)=sin⁡t⋅12+t2cos⁡t⋅1=12(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t).

Finally, evaluating the above at t=π2, we obtain ddt[f(r(π2))]=12(sin⁡(π2)+π2cos⁡(π2))=12(1+π2⋅0)=12.

q-167500.name: Question 16
q-167500.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},\frac{1}{t},t⟩$ at the point $t=\frac{\pi }{4}.$
q-167500.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z)),\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy+z))⟩ \\  & =⟨-y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z),-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy+z)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=\frac{1}{t},$ and $z=t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)⟩\cdot ⟨2t,-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}},1⟩ \\  & =(-\frac{1}{t}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 2t+(-{t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot (-\frac{1}{{t}^{2}})+(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\cdot 1 \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=\frac{\pi }{4}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(\frac{\pi }{4}))] & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

q-36247.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+3xyz$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2},t+1,-t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
q-36247.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+3xyz),\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+3xyz)⟩ \\  & =⟨2x+3yz,3xz,3xy⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x={t}^{2},y=t+1,$ and $z=-t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨2({t}^{2})+3(t+1)(-t),3({t}^{2})(-t),3({t}^{2})(t+1)⟩ \\  & =⟨2{t}^{2}-3{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2t,1,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨-{t}^{2}-3t,-3{t}^{3},3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2t,1,-1⟩ \\  & =(-{t}^{2}-3t)\cdot 2t+(-3{t}^{3})\cdot 1+(3{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2})\cdot (-1) \\  & =-2{t}^{3}-6{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{3}-3{t}^{2} \\  & =-8{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =-8{(1)}^{3}-9{(1)}^{2}=-17.\end{aligned}
$$

q-94885.name: Question 18
q-94885.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2t,3t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
q-94885.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

The chain rule in vector form states that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x+y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(x+y)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(x+y)^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2t$ and $y=3t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(2t+3t)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(2t+3t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+(5t)^{2}},\frac{1}{1+(5t)^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)⟩ \\  & =⟨2,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}},\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}⟩\cdot ⟨2,3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}\cdot 2+\frac{1}{1+25{t}^{2}}\cdot 3 \\  & =\frac{5}{1+25{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$

$$

$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+z),\frac{∂}{∂z}(x{e}^{y}+z)⟩ \\  & =⟨{e}^{y},x{e}^{y},1⟩\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{ln}⁡t),{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨t,4t,1⟩\cdot ⟨0,\frac{1}{t},{e}^{t}⟩ \\  & =t\cdot 0+4t\cdot \frac{1}{t}+1\cdot {e}^{t} \\  & =4+{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}

q-36253.problem: Compute the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{t},4t⟩$ at the point $t=1.$
q-36253.worked_solution:
The rate of change of $f(x,y,z)$ with respect to $t$ along the curve $r(t)$ is given by $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))].$ To calculate this, we can use the chain rule.

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))]=∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t).
$$

First, we need to compute $∇f(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)),\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y))⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute $x=2\sqrt{t}$ and $y=4t$ into the above to find $∇f(r(t)):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(r(t)) & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the derivative of $r(t),$ which is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{t}),\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(t))] & =∇f(r(t))\cdot {r}^{′}(t) \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t),-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)⟩\cdot ⟨\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}},4⟩ \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)\cdot 4 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{t}-4t)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}-4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $f$ along the curve $r(t)$ at $t=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}[f(r(1))] & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{1}-4\cdot 1)(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}-4) \\  & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$
